name: MC9S08QG4CDTE
title: MC9S08QG8 and MC9S08QG4 8-bit HCS08 microcontrollers, 20 MHz CPU, 8 or 4 Kbytes FLASH
summary: An 8-bit HCS08 microcontroller family whose CPU runs at up to 20 MHz (10 MHz bus), with 8 Kbytes of FLASH and 512 bytes of RAM (MC9S08QG8) or 4 Kbytes and 256 bytes (MC9S08QG4), in 8-pin and 16-pin packages. On chip are a 10-bit ADC of up to 8 channels with a temperature sensor and bandgap channel, an analog comparator, SCI, SPI, IIC, a 2-channel 16-bit TPM, an 8-bit modulo timer, keyboard interrupts, an internal FLL clock source trimmed to 0.2 % steps, a crystal oscillator, a COP watchdog and low-voltage detection, with single-wire background debug. MC9S08QG4CDTE is the 4 Kbyte part in the 16-pin TSSOP for -40 °C to 85 °C.

pins.name: PTA5/IRQ/TCLK/RESET
pins.function: Input-only port pin PTA5. Alternates: IRQ external interrupt input (optional internal pull-up), TCLK external clock for the TPM and MTIM, and active-low RESET (set by RSTPE; internal pull-up switched on). A general-purpose input after power-on reset. Has no clamp diode to VDD and must not be taken above VDD; its pulled-up level does not read as VDD. In stop1 and stop2 it is always the active-low wake-up input with its pull-up off, so it needs an external drive or pull-up high.

pins.name: PTA4/ACMPO/BKGD/MS
pins.function: Output-only port pin PTA4. Alternates: ACMPO comparator output, BKGD single-wire background debug, and MS mode select (held low through power-on reset or a background debug force reset to enter active background mode). Comes up as BKGD/MS with its internal pull-up after every reset; BKGDPE must be cleared to use PTA4 or ACMPO.

circuits.description: The connections nearly every design needs. A 3 V supply feeds VDD with a 10 µF bulk capacitor and a 0.1 µF ceramic bypass beside the pins. operation.text: HCS08 CPU at up to 20 MHz running the HC08 instruction set plus BGND. Debug is over one wire: the background controller gives one breakpoint, and the on-chip debug module two more, with two comparators, nine trigger modes and an eight-deep FIFO of change-of-flow addresses or event data, using tag or force breakpoints. Up to 32 interrupt and reset sources.

ADC: 8 channels, 10 bits, automatic compare, asynchronous clock, temperature sensor and internal bandgap channel, and hardware triggering from the RTI counter. ACMP: analog comparator that can compare against an internal reference and route its output to the TPM. SCI with 13-bit break option, SPI, IIC. TPM: two channels, each usable for capture, compare, or buffered PWM aligned to the edge or the center. MTIM: 8-bit modulo timer with 8-bit prescaler. KBI: 8 pins, polarity chosen in software, edge or edge-and-level detection.

ICS: a frequency-locked loop on an internal or external reference; the internal reference trims in 0.2 % steps and stays within 2 % over temperature and voltage; bus clocks from 1 MHz to 10 MHz. XOSC: low-power oscillator for a crystal or ceramic resonator in a 31.25 kHz to 38.4 kHz range or a 1 MHz to 16 MHz range, or an external clock up to 20 MHz on EXTAL.

COP watchdog reset clocked from a dedicated 1 kHz internal source or the bus clock; a low-voltage detector that can reset or interrupt; reset on an illegal opcode or an illegal address; FLASH block protection.

Twelve general-purpose I/O pins plus an input-only and an output-only pin. Each output gives 10 mA, with 60 mA the most for the package. Pull-ups on inputs, and slew rate and drive strength on outputs, are chosen in software. RESET and IRQ have internal pull-ups.

ICSOUT divided by 2 is BUSCLK, which clocks every module register, the CPU, the BDC and the FLASH. ICSFFCLK divided by 2 gives the fixed-frequency clock XCLK for the TPM and MTIM. ICSERCLK, present only with the XOSC, can clock the RTI; a separate 1 kHz clock serves the COP and RTI. ICSLCLK is the alternate BDC clock. TCLK is an external clock pin for the TPM and MTIM. The ADC has minimum and maximum clock limits and the FLASH a clock range for program and erase.

VDD and VSS feed the I/O buffers, the ACMP and ADC, and an internal regulator that supplies the CPU and the rest of the logic at a lower voltage. Usual practice is a bulk capacitor, such as a 10 µF tantalum, for the whole system plus a 0.1 µF ceramic bypass as close to the power pins as practical. Inside the part, VDDA and VREFH are tied to VDD, and VSSA and VREFL to VSS.

operation.topic: Clock after reset and the oscillator
operation.text: Out of reset the ICS runs from its internal reference, nominally 16 MHz, giving a 4 MHz bus. The XOSC is a Pierce oscillator; RANGE in ICSC2 picks its frequency range. RF and RS must be low-inductance (carbon composition, not wire-wound or some metal film). RF, typically 1 MΩ to 10 MΩ, biases EXTAL into its linear region during start-up: higher values are humidity-sensitive, lower values cut gain and at the extreme stop start-up. C1 and C2, usually 5 pF to 25 pF and equal, are high-frequency ceramics sized so their series value, plus about 10 pF of pin and board capacitance per pin, meets the crystal's load capacitance.

After power-on reset PTA5 is a general-purpose input. Setting RSTPE in SOPT1 makes it RESET until the next power-on reset, active low, with the internal pull-up switched on. The pin has no clamp diode to VDD, so it must not be driven above VDD; the pulled-up pin measures below VDD, and the pull-up must not be used for parts outside the MCU. An external RC filter on RESET suits EMC-sensitive designs.

During power-on reset or a background debug force reset, PTA4 is the mode select input; straight after any reset it is BKGD, with BKGDPE set and the internal pull-up on, and BKGDPE must be cleared to use PTA4 or ACMPO. Left open, the part starts in normal mode at the rising edge of internal reset; a debugger on the 6-pin header can hold it low to start in active background mode. The BDC protocol takes 16 BDC clock cycles per bit and the BDC clock can be as fast as the bus, so the pin must carry no significant capacitance. The pin is pseudo open-drain; the protocol adds short driven speed-up pulses, so cable capacitance and the pull-up value hardly change its edges.

Up to 12 I/O plus an input-only and an output-only pin, shared with the peripherals. Outputs have two drive strengths and optional slew limiting; inputs have optional pull-ups. After reset every pin except the output-only one is a high-impedance input with its pull-up off; the output-only function is off, set to low drive with slew control on, and PTA4 is BKGD/MS. Floating inputs draw extra current, so start-up code must enable pull-ups or make unused pins outputs; on 8-pin parts this includes the port B pins that are not bonded out.

Pull-up, slew and drive are set per pin in high-page registers, apart from the port data registers. A pull-up (PTxPEn) is turned off whenever the pin is an output or under an analog function; a KBI pin set for rising edges turns its pull-up into a pull-down. Slew control (PTxSEn) slows output edges to cut emissions and does nothing on inputs. High drive (PTxDSn) raises source and sink current, but the chip's total current limits still apply; it also lets a pin drive a larger load at the same edge speed, which can raise emissions.

When an alternate function is first switched on the module may see a false edge, so clear its flags before enabling its interrupt. The highest-priority enabled function owns the pin, and enabling a higher one over a lower one can give the lower one false edges; disable every module on a pin before enabling another.
Selected when the part leaves reset with BKGD/MS high; execution starts at the address held in 0xFFFE:0xFFFF.

Entered when BKGD/MS is low during power-on reset or just after a background debug force reset, on a BACKGROUND command, on a BGND instruction, or at a BDC or DBG breakpoint. The CPU then waits for serial commands. Non-intrusive commands (memory access, memory access with status, BDC register access, BACKGROUND) work while the program runs; active background commands (CPU register access, single-step, GO) only in this mode. Parts ship with FLASH erased, so this mode loads the first program; it also erases and reprograms the FLASH later.

A WAIT instruction stops the CPU clock and clears the I bit; an interrupt wakes it, starting with the stacking for the service routine. System clocks keep running and full regulation is kept. Only BACKGROUND and memory-access-with-status commands work in wait; the latter report the mode instead of accessing memory, and BACKGROUND wakes the part into active background mode.

A STOP instruction with STOPE set in SOPT1 enters one of three stop modes, chosen by ENBDM, LVDE, LVDSE, PDC and PPDC; bus and CPU clocks halt, and the ICS may keep its reference clocks running. Stop1 powers down nearly everything for the least current. Stop2 powers down all but the RAM. Stop3 keeps every circuit powered for a fast return, holding RAM and registers. With STOPE clear, STOP causes an illegal opcode reset.

Registers, logic, RAM and pin states are kept. RESET, or an interrupt from the RTI, LVD, ADC, IRQ or KBI, ends it; reset takes the reset vector, an interrupt its own vector. With LVDE and LVDSE both set when STOP runs, the regulator stays active and the LVD can still reset or interrupt; the ADC works in stop3 only with the LVD left on. With ENBDM set, the debug clocks and full regulation stay on so background communication continues; most commands then fail but BACKGROUND wakes the part.

Everything except the RAM powers down, and the pin control signals are latched so the pins keep their states. PTA5 is always an active-low wake-up input in stop2, whatever its configuration, with its pull-up off, so it needs an external drive or pull-up to stay high; the RTI can also wake the part. Waking acts like a power-on reset: registers reset, the LVD reset is on with the low trip point and holds reset while VDD is below it, and the reset vector is taken. PPDF in SPMSC2 is set and the pins stay latched until 1 is written to PPDACK. Before that write, software restores the port registers it saved in RAM and re-enables the peripherals that own pins; otherwise the pins fall to their reset states or to port control.

Almost all circuits power down for the lowest standby current and every pin returns to its reset state. PTA5 is the active-low wake-up input with its pull-up off and must be held high externally; the RTI can also wake the part. Waking acts like a power-on reset (registers reset, LVD reset at the low trip point, reset vector), and PDF in SPMSC2 is set until 1 is written to PPDACK.
In every stop mode the clocks to the peripherals stop, even when ENBDM keeps the debug logic clocked.
RAM, FLASH and the I/O and control registers share one 64 Kbyte space. Registers fall in three blocks: direct page 0x0000 to 0x005F, high page 0x1800 to 0x184F, and nonvolatile 0xFFB0 to 0xFFBF.

With KEYEN = 1 an 8-byte key lets code running from secure memory unlock security for the time being; the key cannot be entered by background commands. With KEYEN = 0 the only way out is a mass erase (usually through the background interface) and a blank check. Programming SEC01:SEC00 to 1:0 keeps the part unsecured after the next reset.

Static RAM; addresses below 0x0100 are reachable by direct addressing and by the bit instructions BCLR, BSET, BRCLR and BRSET, which suits the most-used variables. RAM keeps its data in wait, stop2 and stop3 and through any reset as long as VDD stays above VRAM; at power-on and after stop1 it holds unknown values and is not cleared by reset. SP starts at 0x00FF for M68HC05 compatibility; start-up code usually moves it to the top of RAM (LDHX #RamLast+1 then TXS). With security on, RAM is unreachable from BDM or from code in unsecured memory.

Program storage, programmable in circuit through the single-wire background interface, or by the application over any channel since no special voltage is needed. MC9S08QG8: 8,192 bytes in 16 pages of 512 bytes; MC9S08QG4: 4,096 bytes in 8 pages of 512 bytes. Single-supply program and erase, a command interface, rated for 100,000 program/erase cycles (typical supply and temperature), block protection, security for FLASH and RAM, and automatic power-down for slow reads. Reads, programs and erases across the full operating voltage and temperature.
FCDIV must set the FLASH clock to 150 kHz to 200 kHz before any command is taken. FCDIV can be written once, normally at start-up, and not while FACCERR is set.

With FCDIV set and error flags clear: (1) write any data to an address in the array, which latches address and data (any address within the 512-byte block to be erased for a page erase, any FLASH address for mass erase and blank check; data does not matter for erase and blank check); (2) write the command code to FCMD; (3) write 1 to FCBEF in FSTAT to launch. Writing 0 to FCBEF before launch aborts and sets FACCERR. FCCF shows completion. Wait at least four bus cycles after launch before reading FCBEF or FCCF. A 512-byte page is the smallest erasable block, and a byte must not be programmed twice between erases, since that can disturb stored data.

Burst program keeps the FLASH charge pump on between bytes when the next burst command is queued before the current one finishes and the next address lies in the same 64-byte row (A5 to A0 select the byte; a row starts where they are all zero). The first byte, and the first byte of each new row, take the normal byte time; the rest take the burst time. If no command is queued in time, the pump turns off.

FACCERR is set, and must be cleared by writing 1 to it before any new command, by: writing to FLASH before FCDIV is set; writing to FLASH while FCBEF is clear; a second array write or a second FCMD write before launch; after the array write, a write to a FLASH control register that is not FCMD; a command code other than 0x05, 0x20, 0x25, 0x40 or 0x41; touching any FLASH register other than the FSTAT launch write after writing FCMD; entering stop while a command runs (it is aborted); a program (byte or burst) or page-erase command sent through BDM while secured (only blank check and mass erase are allowed then); and writing 0 to FCBEF to cancel.

FPROT protects a region from any 512-byte boundary up to 0xFFFF against program and erase. It is loaded from NVPROT at reset and cannot be written by application code, only by background commands, so a protected part can still be erased and reprogrammed through BDM. NVPROT sits in the last 512 bytes, so any protection also protects NVPROT. A protected boot loader survives a power loss during reprogramming of the rest.

Programming FNORED in NVOPT (0xFFBF) to 0, with part but not all of the FLASH protected through NVPROT (0xFFBD), moves the interrupt vectors 0xFFC0 to 0xFFFD to the same offsets just below the protected block; the reset vector 0xFFFE:FFFF stays put. New vectors can then be programmed without unprotecting the boot area.

With security engaged, FLASH and RAM are secure; registers and the BDC are not. Code in secure memory reaches everything; accesses from unsecured memory or background debug are blocked (writes ignored, reads return 0). SEC01:SEC00 in FOPT, copied from NVOPT at reset, set it: 1:0 is unsecured and the other three states, including the erased 1:1, are secure, so after an erase during development SEC00 is programmed to 0 at once. A secure part blocks the debug module and enters active background mode only when BKGD/MS is held low as reset ends. Backdoor unlock with KEYEN = 1: set KEYACC in FCNFG, write the eight key bytes to NVBACKKEY to NVBACKKEY+7 in order (not with STHX, the writes cannot be on adjacent bus cycles), clear KEYACC; a match sets SEC01:SEC00 to 1:0 until the next reset. The key lives in the same 512-byte block as the vectors, so protecting that block protects the key. Through BDM security is always removable: clear block protection by writing FPROT, mass erase if needed, and blank check; an erased part is unsecured until the next reset.

Reset loads most registers with initial values and the PC from 0xFFFE:0xFFFF, disables the peripherals, makes I/O pins high-impedance inputs without pull-ups, sets the I bit and forces SP to 0x00FF. Sources: external RESET pin (enabled by RSTPE), power-on reset, low-voltage detect, COP timeout, illegal opcode, illegal address, and background debug force reset; all but the last have a flag in the reset status register SRS.

Enabled by COPE after every reset; clearing COPE turns it off. Writing any value to the SRS address clears the counter without changing SRS. COPCLKS in SOPT2 picks the 1 kHz internal clock or the bus clock, and COPT in SOPT1 a short or long timeout; the default is the 1 kHz clock with the long timeout (2^8 cycles). SOPT1 and SOPT2 are write-once, so start-up code writes them even with default values to lock them, which also clears the counter. The clearing write must not sit in an interrupt routine. The counter does not run in background debug mode. On the bus clock it pauses during stop; on the 1 kHz clock it restarts from zero on entering stop.

A hardware event sets a read-only flag; with its local enable set and the I bit clear, the CPU finishes the current instruction, stacks PCL, PCH, X, A and CCR, sets I, fetches the vector of the highest-priority pending source and fills its three-byte instruction queue. RTI restores CCR, A, X and PC. H is not stacked (M68HC08 compatibility), so a service routine pushes and pulls H itself if it changes it. The flag must be cleared before returning, usually at the start of the routine. Clearing I inside a routine to allow nesting is possible but not advised. SWI is an instruction and is not masked by I; the debug module can also cause an SWI.

Stacked toward lower addresses in this order: PCL, PCH, X, A, CCR. Before the interrupt SP points to the next free byte; afterwards it points one below the saved CCR. The stacked PC is the next instruction of the interrupted program.

Enabled by IRQPE in IRQSC. IRQMOD chooses edge-only or edge-plus-level detection, and the pin either interrupts or only sets IRQF for polling. An asynchronous path lets it wake the part from stop. The internal pull-up is on by default (IRQPDD = 0) and IRQPDD = 1 removes it for an external one. BIH and BIL test the pin level. In edge and level mode IRQF cannot be cleared while the pin stays asserted. The pin has no clamp diode to VDD and must not be driven above it; its pull-up is not for external parts.

A power-on reset circuit plus an LVD with a high (VLVDH) or low (VLVDL) trip point chosen by LVDV in SPMSC3, enabled by LVDE in SPMSC1. The LVD turns off in stop unless LVDSE is set; with LVDE and LVDSE both set, stop1 and stop2 are not available and stop3 draws more current. Below VPOR the POR circuit resets the part and the LVD holds reset until VDD passes VLVDL; POR sets both the POR and LVD bits in SRS. With LVDRE = 1 a low voltage resets the part and reset holds until VDD passes the LVDV level. With LVDE and LVDIE set and LVDRE clear it sets LVDF and interrupts instead.
A flag with no interrupt, set when VDD nears but is still above the LVD level; LVWV in SPMSC3 chooses the high (VLVWH) or low (VLVWL) warning level.

Periodic interrupts from the 1 kHz internal clock or, on parts with the XOSC, the external clock, chosen by RTICLKS in SRTISC. Either works in run, wait and stop3 (the external oscillator in stop3 needs EREFSTEN = 1 and RANGE = 0); only the 1 kHz clock can wake the part from stop1 or stop2. RTIS, three bits, picks one of seven periods, and all zeros turns the RTI off; RTIE masks it.

Two ports with 12 I/O pins, one output-only and one input-only (fewer on smaller packages). An enabled peripheral takes the pin from the port logic. After reset all port pins are inputs with pull-ups off, except PTA4, which comes up as BKGD/MS. Unconnected pins need pull-ups or output direction to stop floating-input current.

PTxDDn enables the output buffer and selects what a port data read returns. The input buffer is always on unless an analog function owns the pin or it is output-only. A digital peripheral controls the output buffer, but PTxDDn still selects the read source. An analog function turns both buffers off, and an input bit with its buffer off reads 0. Where a pin has both digital and analog alternates enabled, the analog one wins. Writing the data register before switching a pin to output avoids a glitch of stale data. Reads of PTAD5 always return the PTA5 pin; reads of PTAD4 return the latch.

Stop1: all registers power off and every pin takes its reset state; after waking, pins are set up as after power-on reset. Stop2: latches hold the pins; software saves CPU and I/O state in RAM before STOP, and on waking checks PPDF first: 0 means initialise as after power-on reset; 1 means restore the I/O data from RAM and re-enable the peripherals, then write 1 to PPDACK before using the pins. Stop3: logic stays powered and pins are unchanged.

Source- and object-code compatible upward from the M68HC05 and M68HC08, with added instructions and modes for C code and the background debug system. One 64 Kbyte space for registers and memory; 16-bit stack pointer, so a stack of any size anywhere; 16-bit index register H:X; 8-bit accumulator A, with X usable as a second 8-bit register; seven addressing modes; memory-to-memory moves; V, H, N, Z and C flags for signed, unsigned and BCD branching; bit manipulation; 8 × 8 multiply and 16 ÷ 8 divide; STOP and WAIT.

A: 8-bit accumulator, unchanged by reset. H:X: 16-bit index pointer of two 8-bit halves; some M68HC05-style instructions use only X; reset clears H and leaves X. SP: points to the next free stack byte, forced to 0x00FF at reset; AIS adds a signed 8-bit value to allocate or free locals; RSP only resets the low byte. PC: next instruction address, loaded at reset from 0xFFFE and 0xFFFF. None are in the memory map.

CCR bits, 7 to 0: V, 1, 1, H, I, N, Z, C (bits 6 and 5 always 1). V: two's complement overflow, used by BGT, BGE, BLE, BLT. H: carry from bit 3 to bit 4 in ADD or ADC, used with C by DAA for BCD. I: masks maskable interrupts when 1; set after stacking on an interrupt; after CLI or TAP clears it, interrupts wait one more instruction. N: bit 7 of a result, also on a plain load or store. Z: result 0x00 or 0x0000, also on a plain load or store. C: carry out of bit 7 on add, borrow on subtract, also changed by shifts, rotates and bit-test branches.

The CPU stops at once on a reset event, without waiting for an instruction boundary. When the event ends and RESET is released, a 6-cycle sequence fetches the vector from 0xFFFE and 0xFFFF and fills the instruction queue.

After the current instruction: push PCL first, then PCH, X, A and finally CCR; set I; fetch the high and then the low vector byte; one free bus cycle; fetch three program bytes from the vector address. H is left off the stack: PSHH at the start and PULH before RTI save it, unneeded if the routine cannot change H.

WAIT clears I and stops the CPU clocks until an interrupt or reset. A BACKGROUND command in wait restarts the clocks into active background mode. In stop all clocks, the oscillator included, usually halt, though the HCS08 can keep a minimum clock to wake itself periodically. With a debugger on BKGD and ENBDM set, the oscillator keeps running in stop and BACKGROUND brings the CPU into active background mode.
Stops user code and enters active background mode; the program continues only after reset or a GO, TRACE1 or TAGGO command. Replacing an opcode with BGND makes a software breakpoint.

The ACMP compares two analog pin voltages, or one pin against an internal reference, and works with inputs anywhere from VSS to VDD. With ACIC set in SOPT2 its output feeds TPM input-capture channel 0, and the TPMCH0 pin is then lost to the outside whatever the TPM is set to. Using the bandgap as the plus input needs the bandgap buffer switched on with BGBE = 1 in SPMSC1; the bandgap voltage is in the DC characteristics.

Input offset is under 40 mV and hysteresis under 15 mV. The flag ACF, and an interrupt when ACIE is set, can be raised on a rising output edge, a falling one or either. The output can be read in ACO and can be put out on the ACMPO pin.

In wait mode the comparator keeps running if it was on, so its interrupt can end wait; turn it off when it is not needed then to save current. Every stop mode turns it off, so it cannot wake the part from stop. Stop1 and stop2 remove its power, and it comes back in its reset state. In stop3 its clocks halt, its register keeps its value and the comparator drops into a low-current state with no comparisons made; an interrupt exit resumes where it left off, a reset exit resets it. In active background mode it carries on normally.

ACMP– always drives the inverting input. ACBGS chooses what drives the non-inverting input: the ACMP+ pin (ACBGS = 0) or the internal bandgap reference. The output is high while the non-inverting side is above the inverting side and low while it is below. ACMOD picks which output transition sets ACF: rising, falling or toggle. ACOPE routes the output to the ACMPO pin.
A 10-bit successive-approximation converter. On this part the ADC supply VDDAD and high reference VREFH are joined inside to the VDD pin, and VSSAD and VREFL to the VSS pin.

operation.topic: ADC clocks and trigger on this part
operation.text: The converter can run from the bus clock, the bus clock halved, or its own asynchronous clock ADACK; the ALTCLK input is not connected on this part. The hardware trigger ADHWT is the overflow of the real-time interrupt counter, which runs from ICSERCLK or the RTI's own nominal 1 kHz clock at a period set by RTIS. With the trigger enabled each RTI overflow starts a conversion, in run, wait and stop3. There is one pin-enable register, APCTL1. Converting in stop3 needs LVDSE and LVDE set in SPMSC1.

10-bit linear successive approximation; up to 28 inputs; result right-justified as 10 or 8 bits; single or continuous conversion, returning to idle after a single one; selectable sample time and speed against power; a conversion-complete flag and interrupt; up to four input clock choices; conversion in wait or stop3 for less noise; an asynchronous internal clock; an asynchronous hardware trigger; and an automatic compare that interrupts on a result below, or at or above, a set value.

Where VDDAD is a separate pin it goes to the same potential as VDD, with filtering if needed to keep it clean; VSSAD goes to the VSS potential. VREFH may equal VDDAD or come from a source between the minimum VDDAD and VDDAD, and never above VDDAD. VREFL goes to the VSSAD potential. On this part all four are bonded inside to VDD and VSS. ADCH selects one of up to 28 inputs.

The ADC is off in reset and whenever ADCH is all ones, and sits idle at its lowest current between conversions. The successive approximation yields 11 bits in 10-bit mode and 9 bits in 8-bit mode, rounded to 10 bits in ADCRH:ADCRL or 8 bits in ADCRL. COCO then sets, with an interrupt when AIEN = 1. Setting ACFE adds the automatic compare to any mode.

ADICLK picks the bus clock (the reset choice), the bus clock divided by 2 (allowing up to divide-by-16 with ADIV), ALTCLK, or ADACK, which keeps running in wait and stop3. ADIV then divides by 1, 2, 4 or 8 to make ADCK, which must lie inside the fADCK limits; outside them the converter does not meet its specifications.
Setting a pin-control bit puts that pin's output in high impedance, turns off its input buffer (port reads give 0) and turns off its pull-up.
With ADTRG = 1 a rising edge on ADHWT starts a conversion; an edge during a conversion is ignored, and in continuous mode only the first edge counts.

A conversion starts on a write to ADCSC1 with ADCH not all ones (software trigger), on an ADHWT event (hardware trigger), or, in continuous mode, as soon as the previous result is stored. Continuous conversion runs until aborted.

A conversion finishes when its result reaches ADCRH:ADCRL and COCO sets. If ADCRH has been read but not ADCRL, a new result is held off: COCO stays clear, the result is lost and another conversion starts (except a single compare conversion whose condition is false, which just ends). So after starting a single conversion, leave the result registers unread until it completes, or several conversions may be thrown away at a cost in current. A conversion is aborted by a write to ADCSC1 (a new one starts unless ADCH is all ones), by a write to ADCSC2, ADCCFG, ADCCVH or ADCCVL, by reset, or by entering stop without ADACK. The result registers keep the last good value except after a reset, which clears them.
The ADC idles until a conversion starts, and ADACK runs only when selected. ADLPC lowers active current at the cost of a lower maximum fADCK.

Time depends on ADLSMP (short or long sample), the bus frequency, 8- or 10-bit mode and fADCK. After sampling, the input is cut off and the approximation runs. Continuous conversions with short sampling have a precise sample time only when the bus is at least as fast as fADCK; with long sampling, when the bus is at least fADCK/11.

The result is added to the two's complement of ADCCVH:ADCCVL. With ACFGT = 1 COCO sets when the result is at or above the compare value; with ACFGT = 0, when it is below. The sum, not the raw result, goes to ADCRH:ADCRL. When the condition is false, COCO stays clear and nothing is stored. Used in wait or stop3, the compare interrupt wakes the MCU when the channel crosses the limit.

A conversion under way when WAIT runs finishes, and new ones can start in wait from the hardware trigger or in continuous mode. The bus clock, bus clock/2 and ADACK all work in wait. A completed conversion with AIEN = 1 wakes the MCU.

Without ADACK selected, STOP aborts the conversion and idles the ADC; the result registers keep their value and a fresh trigger is needed after stop3. With ADACK selected the ADC keeps working in stop3 provided the voltage regulator stays on: a conversion in progress completes, the hardware trigger or continuous mode can start more, and completion with AIEN = 1 wakes the MCU. The ADC can also bring the system out of stop3 into run current without an interrupt, so clear the result-blocking condition before entering stop3 with conversions running. Stop1 and stop2 disable the ADC and reset its registers, so it must be set up again afterwards.

Write ADCCFG first (clock source, divider, sample time, low power), then ADCSC2 (trigger type and compare), then ADCSC1 (single or continuous, interrupt enable, channel); the ADCSC1 write starts conversion. A worked case: a single 10-bit low-power long-sample conversion on channel 1 from the bus clock divided by 1 with interrupt is ADCCFG = 0x98, ADCSC2 = 0x00, ADCSC1 = 0x42 and APCTL1 = 0x02. Read ADCRH before ADCRL, which also clears COCO.

Where the analog supply pins are separate, tie them to the digital supply potentials, route them carefully and bypass them close to the package. With separate analog and digital supplies, join their grounds at VSSAD, ideally there and nowhere else. VREFH and VREFL want the same care. Each approximation step draws current spikes through the VREFH–VREFL loop; a 0.1 µF capacitor with good high-frequency behaviour across VREFH and VREFL, at the pins, supplies them. Keep resistance out of that path (the drop causes conversion errors) and its inductance to parasitic only.

Converting works without the pin-control bit set, but setting it avoids contention, removes the pull-up and stops the input buffer drawing DC current at mid-rail levels, so set it on every analog input for lowest current. A 0.01 µF capacitor with good high-frequency behaviour on an input helps with noise or a high source impedance; where fitted it sits at the pin and returns to VSSA. Inputs at or above VREFH read 0x3FF (10-bit) or 0xFF (8-bit); at or below VREFL, 0x000; between, the conversion is linear. VREFL carries a short current while the sample capacitor charges. Sampling lasts 3.5 ADCK cycles with ADLSMP low and 23.5 with it high. Pins next to an analog input should not switch during a conversion.

The input looks like about 7 kΩ and 5.5 pF at most. Settling to 1/4 LSB at 10 bits within the shortest sample window (3.5 cycles at the 8 MHz maximum ADCK) needs a source resistance RAS below 5 kΩ. Higher RAS or better accuracy calls for long sampling (23.5 cycles) or a slower ADCK.

The ADC accuracy figures hold only with: 0.1 µF low-ESR from VREFH to VREFL; 0.1 µF low-ESR from VDDAD to VSSAD; a further 1 µF from VDDAD to VSSAD if the supply is inductively isolated; VSSAD (and VREFL) joined to VSS at a quiet ground point; the MCU in wait or stop3 just before a hardware-triggered conversion or right after any conversion starts (a WAIT or STOP straight after the ADCSC1 write; ADACK as the clock for stop3, which lowers VDD noise but lengthens the effective time); and no I/O switching during the conversion. Where that is not possible, a 0.01 µF CAS from the input to VREFL or VSSAD helps (it slows sampling with the source resistance), averaging helps (four samples remove a single 1 LSB error), and running from ADACK with averaging reduces synchronous noise; noise synchronous with ADCK does not average away.

Zero-scale error EZS is how far the first code's width is from its ideal 1/2 LSB (from 1 LSB if the first code is 0x001). Full-scale error EFS is how far the last code's width is from its ideal 1.5 LSB (1 LSB if the last code is 0x3FE). DNL is the largest departure of any code width from ideal. INL is the peak magnitude reached by DNL summed code by code, the worst gap between a real and ideal transition voltage. TUE is the full difference from the ideal straight-line transfer and includes every error.

Near a transition a steady input can read as either of two codes; the band is about 1/2 LSB and widens with noise, and repeated sampling with averaging, and the measures that hold the ADC accuracy figures, narrow it. In 8-bit and 10-bit modes the ADC is guaranteed monotonic with no missing codes.

The ICS holds a frequency-locked loop steered by the internal or an external reference, and can feed the MCU from the FLL or from either reference directly. It also controls the XOSC oscillator so a crystal or resonator can be the external reference; the external reference is not available in every package. The chosen clock passes through the BDIV divider to become ICSOUT, and the bus runs at half ICSOUT. IREFSTEN (internal reference on in stop) needs LVDE and LVDSE set, but nothing on this part uses the internal reference in stop, so IREFSTEN should be kept 0.

FLL trim resolution of 0.2 % and deviation of 2 % across voltage and temperature, both with the internal 32 kHz reference. Internal or external references up to 5 MHz can steer the FLL, through a reference divider set by 3 bits. The internal reference has 9 trim bits. Either reference can clock the MCU directly. The selected clock can be divided by 1, 2, 4 or 8; the BDC clock is always the DCO output divided by 2. HGO, RANGE, EREFS, ERCLKEN and EREFSTEN control the low-power oscillator. FEI is selected automatically after reset.
No ICS signal leaves the chip.

IREFS = 1 steers the FLL from the internal reference, 0 from the external one (reset value 1). IRCLKEN = 1 puts the internal reference out as ICSIRCLK. IREFSTEN = 1 keeps the internal reference running in stop if IRCLKEN is set or the ICS was in FEI, FBI or FBILP before stop.
In FEI the FLL, steered by the internal reference, gives ICSOUT; ICSLCLK is available to the BDC and the internal reference is on. FEE is the same with the external reference, which is then enabled.

In FBI and FBE, ICSOUT comes straight from the internal or external reference while the FLL stays locked to that reference, so ICSLCLK stays available to the BDC. In FBILP and FBELP the FLL is off and ICSLCLK is not available. The external reference may be a crystal or resonator run by the oscillator, or any external clock.
Entering stop stops every ICS clock, apart from ICSIRCLK when IRCLKEN and IREFSTEN are both 1, and ICSERCLK when ERCLKEN and EREFSTEN are both 1.

IREFS and CLKS can change at any time, together with RDIV so the divided reference stays within 31.25 kHz to 39.0625 kHz. After an IREFS change the FLL relocks within a few cycles of the divided reference. A CLKS change takes effect after a few cycles of the new clock, and does not happen at all if the new clock is absent. A BDIV change takes effect at once.
LP = 1 turns the FLL off in the bypassed modes to save power. Writing LP = 0 lets the FLL run and lock first, for best accuracy before moving into an FLL engaged mode.

With IRCLKEN set the internal reference is also ICSIRCLK. TRIM in ICSTRM sets its period: a larger value slows it, a smaller one speeds it up. TRIM changes ICSOUT in FEI, FBI and FBILP. Reset leaves TRIM and FTRIM unchanged. Before trimming, a low RDIV can push ICSOUT past the chip's maximum frequency. Each device leaves the factory with a trim value in a reserved location that software can copy to ICSTRM at start-up; it does not include FTRIM, which an application trim can set for finer accuracy. With IREFSTEN and IRCLKEN set the reference keeps running in stop for quick recovery.

The ICS accepts an external reference of 31.25 kHz to 5 MHz in every mode. With ERCLKEN set it is also ICSERCLK. When IREFS = 1 the FLL ignores it and it serves only as ICSERCLK, and then it may run as fast as the chip timing allows. With EREFSTEN and ERCLKEN set it keeps running in stop for quick recovery.

The divided FLL reference is offered as ICSFFCLK. ICSFFE is high when ICSOUT is at least four times ICSFFCLK: always in FEI and FEE, and in the bypassed modes only for BDIV = 00 with RDIV ≥ 010, BDIV = 01 with RDIV ≥ 011, BDIV = 10 with RDIV ≥ 100 and BDIV = 11 with RDIV ≥ 101.

After POR the ICS is in FEI with BDIV dividing by 2. The internal reference settles within tIRST, then the FLL locks within tAcquire. The reference needs trimming after POR for an accurate clock; 0xFFAE is the suggested FLASH location for the FTRIM bit (in ICSSC) and 0xFFAF for the 8-bit ICSTRM value. Nothing copies them automatically, so start-up code must. Do not set BDIV to divide by 1 before trimming, or the MCU may run out of specification.

operation.topic: Switching from internal to external clock
operation.text: 1. Turn on the external source in ICSC2, and set LP too if FBE is the target. 2. Wait for it to settle if needed; with EREFS set, OSCINIT sets once the oscillator has finished its start-up cycles (typical crystal start-up times are in the electrical characteristics). 3. Write ICSC1 to pick the mode: for FEE set RDIV and clear IREFS; IRCLKEN may keep the internal reference running for switching back, but leaving it off saves power. 4. Watch CLKST for the switch to finish; for FEE the bus clock is stable after tAcquire. CLKST does not change between FEI and FEE.

operation.topic: Switching from external to internal clock
operation.text: 1. Copy saved TRIM and FTRIM from FLASH to ICSTRM and ICSSC, once after POR. 2. Select FBI (CLKS = 01) or FEI (CLKS = 00, RDIV = 000, IREFS = 1) in ICSC1. 3. Wait for the internal reference to settle (typical start-up time is in the electrical characteristics). 4. Turn off the external clock in ICSC2, or keep it with ERCLKEN for switching back; set LP if FBI is the target. Steps 2 and 3 must come before step 4, since the internal reference has to be running before the external clock stops. 5. Watch CLKST in ICSSC; it does not change between FEE and FEI. For FEI the bus clock is stable after tAcquire.

Two-wire serial bus interface, rated to 100 kbps at full bus loading and timing; with lighter loading it runs faster, up to the module clock divided by 20. Bus capacitance of at most 400 pF limits length and the number of devices. IICPS in SOPT2 moves SDA and SCL between port A and port B.

Slave: write the slave address to IICA, then enable the module and its interrupt in IICC. Master: set the baud rate in IICF, enable the module and interrupt in IICC, set TX, then MST, then write the target address to IICD; the address byte's LSB chooses master receive or transmit. One interrupt routine can serve both roles: a slave transfer begins when a matching address arrives, a master transfer when IICD is written.

On each interrupt clear IICIF, then branch on master or slave. Master transmit: after the last byte, or when no acknowledge came back (RXAK = 1), generate a stop (MST = 0); at the end of the address cycle of a master receive, switch to receive and do a dummy read of IICD; otherwise write the next byte to IICD. Master receive: before the second-last byte is read set the no-acknowledge bit, before the last byte generate a stop, and in every case read IICD and store the byte. Slave: if arbitration was lost, clear ARBL and return unless IAAS = 1. IAAS = 1 is the address phase: SRW = 1 (read) sets transmit and writes the first data byte, SRW = 0 (write) sets receive and does a dummy read. IAAS = 0 is a data phase: when transmitting, send the next byte if the receiver acknowledged, or else switch to receive and do a dummy read; when receiving, read IICD and store the byte.

Compatible with the IIC bus standard; multi-master; 64 software-selected serial clock rates; software-selected acknowledge bit; byte-by-byte interrupt-driven transfer; lost-arbitration interrupt with automatic change from master to slave; calling-address interrupt; START and STOP generation and detection; repeated START generation; acknowledge generation and detection; bus-busy detection.

Normal and monitor modes behave alike. In run, disable the module to save power. In wait it keeps working and can wake the MCU. In stop3 it is inactive and STOP leaves its registers alone; stop1 and stop2 reset them.
SCL is the bidirectional bus clock line and SDA the bidirectional bus data line.

Every device on SDA and SCL must have an open-drain or open-collector output; external pull-ups, sized for the system, make each line a wired AND. A transfer is a START, the slave address, data, and a STOP (the bus STOP, not the CPU instruction).

With both lines high the bus is free, and a master starts by pulling SDA low while SCL is high, which wakes every slave. The first byte is a 7-bit calling address plus R/W (1: slave sends to master; 0: master sends to slave). Only the matching slave acknowledges by holding SDA low on the ninth clock; no two slaves may share an address, and the module as master must not call its own slave address. It cannot be master and slave at once, but after losing arbitration in an address cycle it drops to slave and still answers if addressed. Each data byte is 8 bits, MSB first, one SCL pulse per bit, SDA changing only while SCL is low, then a ninth acknowledge bit from the receiver: nine clocks per byte. A slave that does not acknowledge leaves SDA high; a master receiver that does not acknowledge tells the slave the transfer is over and the slave lets go of SDA. Either way the master then sends a STOP or a repeated START.

A STOP is SDA rising while SCL is high, and frees the bus; the master may send one even after the slave has acknowledged, and the slave must then release the bus. A repeated START is a START with no STOP before it, used to address another slave or change direction without giving up the bus.

With several masters, the shared SCL low time is the longest of their low times and the high time the shortest of their high times. A master sending 1 while another sends 0 loses arbitration, at once becomes a slave receiver and stops driving SDA, with no STOP produced, and a status bit records the loss. Because SCL is wired-AND, a high-to-low edge resets every device's low count; the line stays low until the device with the longest low period lets go, and the first device to finish its high period pulls it low again.
A slave may hold SCL low after a byte (9 bits) to pause the master until it is ready, or stretch individual low periods to slow the bit rate.

Reset disables the IIC, and the IIC never resets the MCU. It has a single interrupt, from IICIF when IICIE is set; software clears IICIF by writing 1 to it and reads the status register to see the cause.

TCF sets on the falling edge of the ninth clock, marking the end of a byte. IAAS sets when the calling address matches the module's own address; the CPU then checks SRW and sets transmit to suit. ARBL sets when arbitration is lost: SDA read low while the master drives high in an address or data transmit cycle, or in the acknowledge bit of a data receive; a START tried while the bus is busy; a repeated START asked for in slave mode; or a STOP seen that the master did not request. Software clears ARBL by writing 1.
The KBI gives up to eight separately enabled external interrupt inputs.

Up to eight pins, each with its own enable. Each pin is either edge-only (falling, or rising) or edge-and-level (falling and low, or rising and high). One interrupt with a software enable. Wakes the MCU from low-power modes.

Left enabled, the KBI keeps working in wait and runs asynchronously in stop3, so an enabled pin with KBIE = 1 can end either. In stop1 and stop2 the KBI is off (its pins may still wake the part through the stop-mode wake path) and it comes back reset. In active background mode it works normally.

KBIPEn = 1 enables pin n as a keyboard interrupt. KBEDGn = 0 picks falling edge or low level for that pin, 1 rising edge or high level. Both registers reset to 0. KBMOD picks edge-only or edge-and-level for all pins.

Besides key matrices, the pins serve as extra interrupt inputs and as a way to wake the MCU from stop or wait. Edges are found synchronously: an enabled input must first sit at its idle level; a falling edge is a 1 in one bus cycle followed by a 0 in the next, a rising edge the reverse.

A valid edge (or level, in edge-and-level mode) sets KBF, and with KBIE set the CPU is interrupted. Writing 1 to KBACK clears KBF; in edge-and-level mode it stays set while any enabled pin is still at its active level.
An internal resistor is turned on through the port's pull-up enable register; KBEDGn then makes it a pull-up (0) or a pull-down (1).
Enabling a pin can raise a false flag, so: clear KBIE; set KBEDGn in KBIES; set any pull resistors in PTxPE; set the KBIPEn bits; write KBACK to clear stray flags; then set KBIE.

The MTIM is an 8-bit up-counter, free-running or counting to a modulo value, with a selectable clock and an overflow interrupt for periodic timing. Its external clock TCLK on PTA5 is chosen with CLKS = 11 or 10 in MTIMCLK, and TCLK can clock the MTIM and the TPM at the same time.

8-bit up-counter, free-running or with an 8-bit modulo limit, software-enabled overflow interrupt, counter reset bit TRST and stop bit TSTP. Four prescaler sources: rising edges of the bus clock, rising edges of XCLK (the fixed-frequency clock), or rising or falling edges of TCLK. Nine prescale ratios: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256.

operation.topic: MTIM in low-power and debug modes
operation.text: In wait it keeps counting and its overflow interrupt can end wait; stop it in wait when not needed to save current. Every stop mode disables it, so it cannot wake the part from stop. After stop1 or stop2, or a reset out of stop3, it is reset; after an interrupt out of stop3 it resumes from its count. In active background mode it pauses and then resumes from the same count unless TRST was written 1 or MTIMMOD written.
TCLK is synchronised to the bus clock and must allow for duty-cycle variation and jitter, so it is limited to one quarter of the bus frequency.

The counter is stopped, free-running or modulo. Any reset stops it and clears the count and modulus to 0x00, with the bus clock and divide-by-1 selected; clearing TSTP starts it free-running. A nonzero modulus (0x01 to 0xFF) gives modulo counting. A clock source or prescaler change while running carries on from the current count. On reaching the modulus the counter rolls to 0x00 and sets TOF. Writing MTIMMOD while running clears the count and TOF. TOF clears by reading MTIMSC with TOF set and then writing 0 to TOF; an overflow in between keeps it set. Writing 1 to TRST or writing MTIMMOD also clears TOF. TOIE enables the overflow interrupt; clear TOF before setting TOIE, never set TOIE while TOF = 1.
With PS = 0010 (divide by 4) and MTIMMOD = 0xAA, the count steps 0xA7, 0xA8, 0xA9, 0xAA, then 0x00, and TOF sets on the step from 0xAA to 0x00, interrupting if TOIE = 1.

Write SCIBDH:SCIBDL for the baud rate, SCIC1 for loop or single-wire, 8 or 9 bits, wakeup and parity, SCIC2 for interrupts, receiver and transmitter enables, RWU and SBK, and SCIC3 for the error interrupts, single-wire pin direction and the ninth bits R8 and T8. Then wait for TDRE before writing SCID, and for RDRF before reading it.

Full-duplex NRZ; transmitter and receiver each double-buffered and each with its own enable; 13-bit modulo baud divider; interrupt or polled operation for transmit buffer empty, transmit complete, receive buffer full, overrun, parity, framing and noise errors and idle line; hardware parity; 8- or 9-bit characters; wakeup of the receiver on an idle line or an address mark; a 13-bit break if wanted; selectable transmit polarity. Modes: 8- and 9-bit data, loop, single-wire; the SCI halts in every stop mode.

Transmitter and receiver share one baud generator clocked from the bus. The receiver resynchronises on every high-to-low edge, but a frame of 10 or 11 bits may have none, so mismatch builds up over a whole character. With a crystal-driven bus, about ±4.5 % mismatch is tolerated for 8-bit data and about ±4 % for 9-bit data; the divider usually gets within a few percent of a standard rate.

TxD idles high (TXINV = 0 after reset); TXINV = 1 inverts it. Setting TE sends a preamble of one idle frame. The shift register is 10 bits (start, 8 data, stop) or 11 with M = 1. When it is free, SCID moves into it and TDRE sets; if nothing follows the stop bit, TC sets and TxD stays high. Clearing TE releases the pin only after any character, idle or break in progress or queued has gone.

A break is a whole frame of 0s (10 bit times with start and stop); BRK13 = 1 lengthens it to 13. Writing SBK 1 then 0 after TDRE sets queues one break; if SBK is still 1 when it reaches the shifter another is queued. A Freescale SCI receives a break as all-zero data with a framing error. For idle-line wakeup, a whole idle frame between messages is needed; writing TE 0 then 1 after TDRE queues one. If the shifter might finish while TE = 0, set the TxD port pin as an output driving 1 so the line still idles high.

RE enables it. A frame is a start bit (0), 8 or 9 data bits sent LSB first, then a stop bit (1). After the stop bit the character moves to the receive buffer and RDRF sets, unless the buffer is still full, in which case OR sets and the new character is lost. Double buffering gives one character time to read SCID after RDRF.

The receiver samples at 16 times the baud rate, slots RT1 to RT16 per bit. A start edge is a 0 after three 1s; samples at RT3, RT5 and RT7 confirm it if at least two are 0. Each bit is then the majority of samples at RT8, RT9 and RT10 (the start bit counts as 0 on its RT3/5/7 vote alone). Any disagreeing sample in a frame sets NF. The edge search resynchronises on every falling edge. After a framing error (not a break) the edge detector is preloaded with three 1s so a new start bit is found almost at once, but no new character reaches the buffer until FE is cleared.

A receiver not addressed by a message sets RWU, which suppresses its receive flags; it clears itself at the end of the message or start of the next. WAKE = 0 (idle-line): RWU clears after a whole idle character (10 or 11 bit times as M sets); that idle character sets neither IDLE nor RDRF. ILT = 0 begins counting idle once the start bit is past, so trailing 1s and the stop bit count; ILT = 1 starts it after the stop bit. WAKE = 1 (address mark): RWU clears when the MSB of a received character (bit 8, or bit 9 with M = 1) is 1, which also sets RDRF; messages may then contain idle characters.

Three vectors: transmit (TDRE, TC), receive (RDRF, IDLE) and error (OR, NF, FE, PF), each of the eight sources with its own enable; flags can be polled with the enables off. TDRE means the transmit buffer has room (TIE interrupts). TC means everything, including preamble and break, has gone and TxD is high (TCIE interrupts). RDRF and IDLE clear by reading SCIS1 with the flag set and then SCID; IDLE cannot set again until a new character has set RDRF. NF, FE and PF set together with RDRF for the faulty character; on overrun only OR sets and the character with its error flags is lost.

M = 1 adds a ninth bit above the MSB: T8 for transmit and R8 for receive, both in SCIC3. Write T8 before SCID; it need not be rewritten if unchanged, and it is copied to the shifter with the data. The ninth bit is used for parity, as the address-mark wakeup bit, or as a software marker.
Clocks stop in every stop mode. Stop1 and stop2 lose all SCI registers, which need setting up again; stop3 keeps them and the SCI resumes on exit. Avoid entering stop mid-character.

With LOOPS = 1, RSRC = 0 gives loop mode: the transmitter feeds the receiver inside and RxD returns to general I/O, useful for software checks. RSRC = 1 gives single-wire half duplex: the receiver connects to the transmitter output and the TxD pin, RxD returns to general I/O, and TXDIR sets TxD as input (0) or output (1); the receiver hears what the transmitter sends.

Master or slave; full duplex or single-wire bidirectional; programmable bit rate; double-buffered transmit and receive; selectable clock polarity and phase; an output for slave select; MSB-first or LSB-first.

The master starts every transfer, shifting out on MOSI while shifting in on MISO, so the two shift registers swap contents. SPSCK is driven by the master, and a slave is selected by holding its SS low; a master can use SS as a slave-select output. Like-named pins are wired together: SPSCK to SPSCK, MISO to MISO, MOSI to MOSI. Typical slaves are shift registers for extra I/O and serial A/D or D/A converters, often with data flowing one way only.

Data written to SPID goes to the transmit buffer and into the shifter when a transfer starts; a received byte goes to the receive buffer, read from SPID. As master, the clock goes out on SPSCK, the shifter out on MOSI and in from MISO; as slave, SPSCK clocks in, the shifter drives MISO and reads MOSI.

With SPE = 0 all four pins are general I/O. SPSCK is the clock input as slave and output as master. With SPC0 = 0, MOSI is data out as master and in as slave, and MISO is data in as master and out as slave. With SPC0 = 1 (single-wire): as master MOSI becomes the bidirectional MOMI pin and MISO is free for general I/O; as slave MISO becomes SISO and MOSI is free; BIDIROE sets input (0) or output (1). SS is the active-low select input as slave. As master it is general I/O when MODFEN = 0; with MODFEN = 1, SSOE = 0 makes it the mode-fault input and SSOE = 1 the slave-select output.

operation.topic: SPI transmit flag and data register
operation.text: SPTEF sets when the transmit buffer has room and clears by reading SPIS with SPTEF set and then writing SPID; a write to SPID without that read is ignored. On an idle SPI a written byte passes to the shifter within two bus cycles, so a second byte can be queued at once. MODF sets when, as master with MODFEN = 1 and SSOE = 0, SS goes low; it clears by reading it set and then writing SPIC1. SPID reads the receive buffer and writes the transmit buffer; as master a write starts a transfer. Read the received byte after SPRF sets and before the next transfer ends, or it is overwritten and lost.

The master checks SPTEF = 1 and writes SPID; the byte moves to the shifter, SPTEF sets again and the transfer starts. Data is sampled on one SPSCK edge and the output changes half a cycle later; after eight SPSCK cycles the bytes have been exchanged, the received byte is in the receive buffer and SPRF sets, and a queued byte starts the next transfer. MSB goes first unless LSBFE = 1. A slave's SS must be low before and throughout a transfer; with CPHA = 0 it must return high between bytes, with CPHA = 1 it may stay low. A receive overrun loses the new byte and sets no flag, so the system must read each byte before the next transfer begins.

CPOL inverts the clock and CPHA chooses one of two clock-to-data phase relations, giving four formats. With CPHA = 1 the slave starts driving MISO when SS falls but data is valid only from the first SPSCK edge, which shifts out the first bit; the second edge samples; the third shifts. The master's SS output falls half an SPSCK cycle ahead of the transfer and rises when bit 8 ends. With CPHA = 0 the slave puts its first bit on MISO as SS falls; the first SPSCK edge samples and the second shifts. The master's SS output falls as bit 1 begins and rises half a cycle after bit 8 ends. The SS output behaviour needs MODFEN and SSOE both 1.

One vector, three flags, two enables: SPIE covers SPRF and MODF, SPTIE covers SPTEF. With enables clear the flags can be polled. The service routine should find the cause from the flags and clear them, usually near its start.

With MSTR = 1, MODFEN = 1 and SSOE = 0, SS low means another device is trying to be master. MODF then sets, MSTR clears back to slave, and the SPSCK, MOSI and MISO (unless bidirectional) drivers turn off to avoid a driver clash. Clear MODF by reading it set and then writing SPIC1, and fix the cause before returning to master.

With ACIC set in SOPT2 the comparator output drives input-capture channel 0 and the TPMCH0 pin is not available. CLKSB:CLKSA = 11 in TPMSC selects the external TPMCLK, which is the TCLK pin; TCLK on PTA5 can clock the TPM and the MTIM together.

A 16-bit counter, free-running, modulo, or up/down for centre-aligned PWM, with a clock source select (off, bus clock, XCLK, external) and a prescaler of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64 or 128, plus two channels on this part. TPMMODH:TPMMODL sets the modulus; 0x0000 or 0xFFFF leaves it free-running. The counter can be read at any time without disturbing it, and a write to either byte of TPMCNT clears it. Each channel can be set on its own to capture inputs, compare outputs or make buffered edge-aligned PWM.

A timer input pin can have a passive pull-up. After reset the TPM is off and its pins are general inputs with pull-ups off. The external clock goes through a bus-clocked synchroniser, so it must be under half the bus frequency; the stated upper limit is a quarter of the bus frequency, leaving room for duty cycle and FLL jitter. Where the external clock shares a channel pin, that channel cannot use the pin (it still works as a software output-compare timer) and its ELSnB:ELSnA must be 00. A channel pin is under timer control or general I/O depending on the channel set-up; under timer control the port data and direction bits have no effect.
In output compare and PWM a byte written to TPMCnVH or TPMCnVL waits in a buffer, and the 16-bit value moves in once both bytes are written, in either order; writing TPMCnSC resets this latch.

CPWMS = 1 makes the counter count up and down and puts every channel in centre-aligned PWM; with CPWMS = 0 every channel chooses capture, compare or edge-aligned PWM for itself. After reset CLKSB:CLKSA = 00, no clock, and the TPM is idle; 01 usually selects the bus clock. External clock is limited to a quarter of the bus rate. In active background mode counting pauses; in stop all TPM clocks stop; in wait it runs normally. Counting up, it runs from 0x0000 to 0xFFFF or the modulus and wraps to 0x0000.

In up/down mode it counts up from 0x0000 to the modulus and back down; both ends last one timer clock. TOF, interrupting when TOIE = 1, sets on the wrap to 0x0000 when counting up, and in up/down mode as the count turns down from the modulus, the end of a PWM period (0x0000 is the period's centre). Reading either counter byte freezes both in a buffer until the other is read, while counting goes on; writing either byte clears the counter and this buffer.

With CPWMS = 0, MSnB:MSnA picks the channel mode. In input capture an active edge (rising, falling or either) latches the counter into TPMCnVH:TPMCnVL and sets CHnF, with an optional interrupt. Reading either byte buffers both for a coherent 16-bit read; writing TPMCnSC resets that.
When the counter reaches the channel value the pin can be set, cleared or toggled, and CHnF sets. A new value takes effect only when both bytes are written; writing TPMCnSC resets the sequence.

Uses up-counting (CPWMS = 0) and can share the TPM with capture and compare channels. The modulus sets the period and TPMCnVH:TPMCnVL the pulse width, the time from overflow to compare. ELSnA = 0: overflow drives high and compare drives low; ELSnA = 1 the reverse. A channel value of 0x0000 gives 0 %; a value above the modulus gives 100 %, so 100 % needs a modulus below 0xFFFF. New values take effect once both bytes are written and the counter is at 0x0000, so a new duty cycle starts with the next full period.

Uses up/down counting (CPWMS = 1); keep the modulus between 0x0001 and 0x7FFF, as other values give ambiguous results, and ELSnA sets polarity. A channel value of zero or with bit 15 set gives 0 %; a positive value above the nonzero modulus gives 100 %, so the usable modulus range is 0x0001 to 0x7FFE (0x7FFF if 100 % is not needed). A modulus of 0x0000 must not be used in this mode, as the counter needs a nonzero match to turn round. With ELSnA = 0 the match while counting up drives low and the match while counting down drives high. Centre-aligned outputs switch fewer pins on the same clock edge than edge-aligned ones, giving less noise, and some motor drives need them.

Writes to TPMMODH, TPMMODL, TPMCnVH and TPMCnVL go to buffers and take effect once both bytes are written and the counter turns round at the modulus; output-compare channels do not wait for that. The TOF interrupt at the end of the count lets software reload any of the PWM buffers so they all change together at the next period. Writing TPMSC discards pending modulus bytes and resets their latch; writing TPMCnSC does the same for that channel's value.

There is an optional overflow interrupt and one per channel. A channel flag sets on each selected capture edge, or in compare and PWM on each match with the channel value. Each flag can be polled or enabled (TOIE, CHnIE); an enabled flag holds its interrupt until cleared. Flags clear by reading them while set and then writing 0; a new event in between leaves the flag set.

operation.topic: TPM channel and PWM flag timing
operation.text: For input capture ELSnB:ELSnA picks rising, falling, either or no edge. In output compare the flag sets on each match. In edge-aligned PWM it sets at the end of the active part of the cycle; in centre-aligned PWM the count matches twice per cycle, so it sets at the start and the end of the active part.

Debug uses the background debug controller (BDC), a single-wire link that also programs the FLASH, and the on-chip debug module (DBG), which can trigger on and capture bus activity so a host can rebuild what the CPU did cycle by cycle, since no address or data bus reaches the pins. The BDC gives memory access, register changes, breakpoints and single-step without disturbing the application. Clearing CLKSW in BDCSCR selects ICSLCLK as the alternate BDC clock.

One pin for mode select and communication; BDC registers outside the memory map; a SYNC command to find the communication rate; memory access that does not stop the program; CPU register access in active background mode; GO and TRACE1; BACKGROUND can wake the CPU from stop or wait; one hardware address breakpoint; the oscillator keeps running in stop while the BDC is enabled; the COP is disabled in active background mode.

operation.topic: BDC command groups and host connection
operation.text: The BDC uses no user memory, memory-map location or peripheral. Active background mode commands need the user program halted and read or write CPU registers, trace one instruction, or GO. Non-intrusive commands work at any time and access memory or the BDC's own registers. A host pod, connected by RS-232, parallel port, USB or the like, reaches the target through ground, BKGD, RESET and sometimes VDD. An open-drain RESET connection lets the host reset the target; VDD can power the pod, and a separately powered pod can attach to a running target without resetting it.

BKGD carries commands and data both ways, selects at reset between active background mode and the user program, and answers a SYNC request with a timed pulse. The host starts every bit with a falling edge and sends MSB first at a rate set by the target BDC clock. The pin is pseudo open drain with an on-chip pull-up, so no external pull-up is needed; short actively driven speed-up pulses make rise times fast regardless of the line's RC. With no pod on the 6-pin connector the pull-up selects normal operation. A pod can hold BKGD and RESET low, release RESET to enter active background mode, then release BKGD. Talking to the target does not require a reset.

Each bit takes 16 BDC clock cycles nominally. If 512 BDC cycles pass between host falling edges the link times out and any command in progress is dropped without touching memory or mode. CLKSW chooses the bus clock or the alternate clock as BDC clock, and the host must know that rate. The target sees the start of a bit 0 to 1 cycle after the host's edge.
The target reads the BKGD level 10 BDC cycles after it sees the bit start. The host usually drives BKGD actively high and low while sending, since the target does not drive the line then.

The host pulls BKGD low for at least two target BDC cycles to start the bit, and lets go before the target's speed-up pulse. For a 1, the target drives a short high speed-up pulse 7 cycles after the bit start. For a 0, the target holds BKGD low for 13 cycles and then pulses it high. The host samples about 10 cycles after starting the bit.

The host pulls BKGD low for 128 or more cycles of the lowest BDC clock rate the target could have (normally the reference oscillator or self-clocked rate divided by 64), drives a short high speed-up pulse, releases the pin and watches it. The target waits for BKGD to go high, waits 16 cycles, drives it low for 128 BDC cycles, gives a 1-cycle high speed-up pulse and releases it. The host times the 128-cycle low pulse to set its rate, typically within a few percent, and the protocol tolerates errors of several percent.

One breakpoint compares the CPU address with the 16-bit BDCBKPT. Forced (FTS = 1): the CPU enters active background mode at the first instruction boundary after any access to that address, which may be any address. Tagged (FTS = 0): the opcode at that address is tagged and the CPU enters active background mode instead of executing it when it reaches the end of the queue, so the address must be an opcode. BKPTEN in BDCSCR enables it and is 0 after reset. The DBG module adds two more flexible breakpoints.

The ratings are stress limits only: the part is not guaranteed to work at them, and going past them can damage it or shorten its life. The pins have protection against static discharge, but no voltage above the maximum ratings should be applied. Unused inputs are more reliable tied to VSS or VDD, or with their internal pull-up enabled.

Power in the I/O pins is set by the application, not the MCU, and is usually small next to the power of the on-chip logic and regulator. To include it, multiply each pin's current by the difference between its voltage and VSS or VDD; that difference is very small unless a pin carries a heavy load.

ESD tests follow AEC-Q100 (the automotive stress-test qualification), with human body, machine and charged device model stresses applied during qualification. A device counts as failed when it no longer meets its specification after the pulses; complete DC parametric and functional tests are run at room temperature and then hot, unless the specification says otherwise.
textrst is the low pulse on the RESET pin. tILIH is the low pulse width on IRQ or a falling-edge KBIPx input and tIHIL the high pulse width on a KBIPx input set for rising edges.

Synchronizers clocked at the bus rate set the shortest input pulse the timers can see and the fastest external clock they can count. tTCLK is the TCLK period with high and low parts tclkh and tclkl; tICPW is the shortest high or low pulse on a TPMCHn input-capture pin.

The numbers 1 to 12 in the SPI timing table name the intervals of the master and slave waveforms for CPHA = 0 and CPHA = 1. In master mode SS is an output when DDS7 = 1 and SSOE = 1. With LSBF = 0 the most significant bit goes first; with LSBF = 1 the order is LSB, bit 1 to bit 6, MSB. A slave drives MISO with an undefined level outside the character: after the last bit with CPHA = 0, normally the most significant bit of the character just received, and before the first bit with CPHA = 1, normally its least significant bit.

Seen from the pin, an ADC input is the pad leakage of the input protection, then the input resistance RADIN through the channel select to the sampling capacitance CADIN of the SAR engine; the other channel inputs join through their own RADIN. Outside the MCU the source is VAS behind RAS with stray capacitance CAS, and VADIN is the voltage at the pin.
Programming and erasing need nothing but the normal VDD supply.

EMC performance depends heavily on the surroundings: board design and layout, circuit topology, the placement and nature of the external parts, and the software all matter. Application notes AN2321, AN1050, AN1263, AN2764 and AN1259 cover improving it.

Radiated emissions are measured from 150 kHz to 1 GHz in a TEM or GTEM cell to IEC 61967-2 and SAE J1752/3, with the MCU on a custom EMC board running EMC test software, with the package turned to face North and then East. The levels given are the maximum over all orientations.

Conducted susceptibility is measured by an internal Freescale method with the MCU on a custom EMC board running EMC test software. A transient based on IEC 61000-4-4 (EFT/B) is injected on each pin in turn; the result is the smallest transient voltage that degrades operation on any pin.
